 The best fitness trackers do far more than count steps. Today's wearables can help you understand how well you've slept, whether you're recovered enough to train, how your heart is performing and even when it's time to take a rest day. Better still, you don't need to spend flagship smartwatch money to benefit from those insights.
 The category has evolved dramatically over the last few years, too. Alongside familiar fitness bands, you'll now find lightweight GPS watches, discreet smart rings and even screen-free trackers that quietly collect health data without constantly demanding your attention. Choosing the right one is less about finding the device with the longest feature list and more about finding the one that fits your lifestyle.
 Our team has spent more than a decade testing fitness trackers, smartwatches and wearable technology from Garmin , Apple , Fitbit , Samsung , Amazfit and many more. We judge every device on tracking accuracy, battery life, comfort, software, training tools and overall value, wearing each one for weeks before deciding whether it deserves a place in this guide.

 If the idea of wearing a fitness tracker without another screen in your life appeals, the Garmin Cirqa is the best screenless option we've tested. It quietly tracks your activity, sleep and recovery throughout the day, then surfaces everything in the excellent Garmin Connect app when you're ready to check in.
 The Cirqa takes a more hands-off approach to fitness tracking than a smartwatch. It fades into the background between workouts, quietly logging your sleep, heart rate and recovery without another screen demanding your attention. When you do want to exercise, the tactile button makes starting and stopping a workout quick and reassuringly simple, and we found its heart rate and sleep tracking more than capable for day-to-day training.
 It isn't cheap, and for similar money you could pick up an entry-level Garmin watch such as the Forerunner 165 , which offers built-in GPS and more advanced training features. However, if your goal is to spend less time looking at a screen while still benefiting from Garmin's health insights, the Cirqa makes a strong case for itself. 
The free Garmin Connect app includes all the core health and fitness metrics most people need, while the optional Connect+ subscription (£6.99 / $6.99 per month) adds AI-powered insights, extra coaching and a handful of premium features. That also gives the Cirqa an edge over Whoop, whose subscription is mandatory rather than optional, making Garmin's tracker the more affordable choice over the long term.

 How to choose the best fitness tracker 
 When choosing a fitness tracker, start by thinking about how you exercise. If you're mainly interested in tracking daily activity, sleep and general wellness (such as recovery, stress, heart health and overall activity levels), a simple fitness band or screenless tracker may be all you need. However, if you run, cycle or spend a lot of time training outdoors, it's worth looking for a device with built-in GPS so it can accurately track your routes and pace without relying on your phone.
 Next, consider how much data you actually want. Some trackers focus on simple metrics like steps, heart rate and sleep, while others provide detailed training analysis, recovery insights and personalised coaching. More information isn't always better, so think about whether you'll use those extra metrics before paying for them.
 Comfort matters too. A fitness tracker proves the most useful when you wear it consistently, so it's worth considering how it will fit into your everyday life. If you already wear a traditional watch, a smart ring such as the Samsung Galaxy Ring or a screenless tracker like the Google Fitbit Air or Amazfit Helio Strap can be a good alternative, offering health and activity tracking without adding another watch-sized device to your wrist.
 Finally, think about the display. Devices with bright AMOLED screens are generally easier to read at a glance and outdoors in bright sunlight, while simpler fitness bands often prioritise battery life over display quality. If you plan to check your stats regularly throughout the day, a larger, sharper screen may be worth the extra cost.
 What is a fitness tracker?
 A fitness tracker is a device, typically a wristband, that monitors statistics such as your heart rate, the number of steps you take each day, and how long you spend working out. You might think of Fitbit bands as the quintessential tracker, but Apple Watches and other devices, such as smart rings, are fitness trackers too. 
 Most fitness trackers have several dedicated modes for recording different forms of exercise, and some also have GPS for tracking your location during runs, walks and bike rides. Most fitness trackers also monitor how long you spend sleeping, and in each sleep stage.
 All this data is sent to an app on your smartphone, where you can track changes over time. Most apps give you virtual 'awards' for achieving particular goals, such as taking 10,000 steps per day or going to bed on time.
 Why do you need a fitness tracker?
 It can be tough to break old habits and develop new ones, and a fitness tracker can help give you the encouragement you need. Tracking the number of steps you take each day and aiming for a particular target might be simple, but it can push you to make simple changes (like getting off the bus a stop earlier, or walking short distances rather than driving), which can add up to make a significant difference over time.
 Which fitness trackers are most accurate?
 Most modern fitness trackers do an excellent job in tracking heart rate, stress and sleep accurately. Fitness trackers have optical heart rate sensors that can keep up with quick changes in heart rate. 
 Some have GPS to better track running, walking and cycling workouts outdoors. This is generally an estimation, but if you run, walk or cycle frequently and want to closely track those workouts, it's best to choose a tracker with GPS as it can monitor your routes, distance travelled, and speed. 
 Check our full reviews for more information: we test fitness trackers against each other and industry gold standards, such as the Apple Watch Ultra 3 or Polar H10 heart rate monitor , to determine whether there are significant differences in GPS and heart rate readings.
 What makes a good fitness tracker?
 A good fitness tracker is one that you'll wear every day and will help you build up a complete picture of your health. With that knowledge, you can start to make small tweaks that will help you sleep better, lower your resting heart rate, improve your fitness, and generally feel better. 
 How we test the best fitness trackers 
 Battery
 During testing we extensively study the battery life of all these devices. Simply wearing them for a few days isn't enough, so we always make sure to run them down completely to get a true feel for how long battery lasts in a given fitness tracker. Obviously your mileage may vary, but we always use them the way most regular people would to give a fair assessment.
 Health tracking and accuracy
 All of our reviewers have extensive experience with fitness and health tracking tech, so we know what to look for when it comes to calorie tracking, heart rates, and sleep. We even test these devices alongside existing tech to look for disparity and erratic results.
 Workouts
 Obviously, we undertake extensive fitness tracking to test the best fitness trackers, conducting a variety of workouts including running and cycling. All of our reviewers engage in a variety of different sports, together they bring years of experience and a huge variety of disciplines to the table.

 If you have an iPhone and want a smartwatch, the Apple Watch is the obvious place to start. But obvious doesn't always mean best. Garmin , Amazfit and Huawei all make watches that work with iOS, and some have clear advantages over Apple 's own models, from longer battery life to more detailed running stats.
 We've tested smartwatches across these brands to find out what you gain and lose by choosing each one. That means looking at how well they pair with an iPhone, which health and fitness features you can actually use, and whether the companion app makes it easy to get at your data.
 Your priorities matter, too. If you run regularly, you may want proper training metrics and recovery advice. If you mainly want to track sleep, check notifications and keep an eye on your heart rate, you might not need to spend Apple Watch money. Battery life is another key consideration, especially if you'd rather not charge your watch every night.

 The Apple Watch Series 12 is our favourite smartwatch for iPhone users, and there's more to it than seeing notifications on your wrist. Its biggest new feature is Readiness Score, which uses your sleep and other health data to give you a score out of 10, helping you gauge how ready you might feel for the day ahead.
 Our reviewer spent more than a month testing the Series 12 and found Readiness Score the addition he used most. The redesigned sensors collect heart-rate and heart-rate variability data more frequently, helping to inform that score. Better still, it's included in the price, with no subscription needed to access it.
 The S11 chip keeps everything running smoothly, and the always-on OLED display makes checking your stats straightforward. Battery life is rated for up to 24 hours, and faster charging helps when you're short on time. Our reviewer did experience two overnight shutdowns, so a quick charge before bed is worth building into your routine if you want to track your sleep.
 If you're using an Apple Watch Series 9 or older, the new health features give you a good reason to consider upgrading. Series 10 and 11 owners can probably hold on to their current watch. For most iPhone users, the Series 12 is a well-rounded choice that covers what matters without the extra bulk of the Ultra 4, which makes more sense if you need a tougher watch and longer battery life for outdoor adventures.

 Battery life is the Apple Watch Ultra 4's biggest strength. In our testing, it lasted around two and a half days between charges, even with the always-on display enabled and sleep tracking running overnight. That's a welcome break from the nightly charging routine, and if you do run low, 15 to 20 minutes on the charger is enough to restore around 30% battery.
 The Ultra 4 has useful health features to match that stamina. Like the Apple Watch Series 12, it gets Apple's new Readiness Score, which uses sleep and activity data to help you decide whether you're primed for a tough workout or might be better off taking it easy. You don't need a subscription to access it, either. The updated health sensors also take heart-rate and heart-rate variability readings more frequently. The latter measures the time between heartbeats and can offer clues about recovery and stress. During our testing, the Ultra 4's average heart-rate reading on a 5km run came within 2bpm of an electrical heart-rate monitor.
 Its rugged 49mm titanium case, bright display and customisable Action Button make it a good companion for outdoor adventures. The button gives you quick access to a chosen function, such as starting a workout, and the S11 chip keeps apps and menus running smoothly.
 The trade-off is size. This is a substantial watch, and it can feel like overkill if you have smaller wrists or simply want something discreet.
 The Ultra 4 sticks with the familiar design of the Ultra 3, refining the experience rather than reinventing it. If you already own last year's model, the changes may not be enough to tempt you to upgrade just yet. For older Apple Watch owners, the Ultra 4 brings longer battery life, smarter health tracking and a rugged build.

 The Apple Watch SE 3 is the Apple Watch we’d point most Apple fans towards if you want the essentials without paying Series 11 or Ultra money. It skips some of the fancier health tools and newer design touches, but when you are saving $100+, it doesn't feel like the biggest compromise.

Our reviewer found it made everyday moments much easier, whether that was quickly checking the time in a meeting or glancing at notifications without doing the slightly awkward wrist flick Apple Watch users know all too well.
 Performance is another big win. The SE 3 runs on the same S10 chip as the pricier Series 11 and Ultra 3, and our reviewer found it just as smooth in daily use. Apps open quickly, watchOS 26 feels snappy, and gestures like Double Tap and Wrist Flick work just as well here as they do on Apple’s more expensive watches.

You miss out on some of Apple’s more advanced health features, including ECG and Blood Oxygen monitoring, and the thicker bezels mean it looks a little less modern than the Series 11 or Ultra 3. Battery life is solid rather than show-stopping, but our reviewer still comfortably got through a full day, even with sleep tracking enabled, and fast charging helps take some of the sting out of daily top-ups.

 How to choose the best smartwatch for iPhone 
 Choosing the best smartwatch for your iPhone requires you to think about compatibility, features, and your priorities. The first thing to consider is compatibility. The Apple Watch is the best smartwatch for most people with an iPhone. It’s designed to work seamlessly with iOS and it offers great integration with Apple’s ecosystem. Features like notifications, messaging, Apple Pay, and health data syncing all work incredibly well. If you want the most out of your smartwatch, for most people an Apple Watch is the top choice.
 Consider the features you need the most. The Apple Watch offers a range of fitness and health tracking, including heart rate monitoring, ECG, sleep tracking, and blood oxygen levels. Newer models now offer even more advanced features, like body temperature tracking. But if health and fitness aren’t your priority, many of the watches in the guide above offer support for notifications, app interactions, and even cellular connectivity for use without your phone.
 The Apple Watch is considered the gold standard for iPhone users, but other options, like Fitbit or Garmin smartwatches, also work very well with iOS. You may find that they don’t offer the same level of integration but do bring you excellent health tracking features and longer battery life. So if you're primarily looking for a fitness tracker with basic notification functionality, these can be great alternatives.
 A downside of the Apple Watch, at least compared to some other brands, is its battery life. It typically lasts a day or two. This means that if you prioritize longer-lasting battery life over advanced features, you may want to consider alternatives from other brands, like Garmin, which can last longer on a single charge, depending on the model.
 Since you’re going to be wearing it most of the time, the design of the smartwatch for iPhone you choose will be a crucial factor. Apple Watches come in a range of sizes and you can customize them with interchangeable bands, which makes it easy to find a style that suits you. Other smartwatch brands also offer nice-looking and comfortable designs, but depending on your preferences, Apple has the edge in terms of aesthetics and comfort.
 For the best overall experience, especially if you have a lot of other Apple products, an Apple Watch is the clear winner. However, if you’re looking for specific features, like extended battery life or more focused fitness tracking, other brands can still offer a solid experience for your iPhone.
 How we test the best smartwatches for iPhone 
 Our smartwatch process typically involves using the device as if it were our own personal wearable. That's the best way for us to fully test it and see how it fares in the real world. We do a comprehensive sweep of its features, functionalities, performance, battery life, and ease of use, doing so over multiple days.
 Of course, since we also want to know how it performs and which features are available when it's paired with an iPhone, we make sure to squeeze that into our testing as well. Once we've collected all the data and information we need, we take all of it and compare it to the smartwatch's price, finding out if it's a great value for our readers before making a recommendation.
 FAQs 
 What's the best smartwatch for iPhone users?
 The best smartwatch for iPhone users is the one that fits your budget and what you expect it to do; at the time of writing, the Apple Watch Series 11 is our best overall pick for its balance of iPhone integration, display, health tools and everyday usefulness. If you want longer battery life and more structured training tools, the Garmin Venu X1 may suit you better, while the Amazfit Active 2 is our budget option.
 We regularly update this guide as we test and review new watches, so the best overall pick can change. If you are not ready to buy yet, bookmark this page and return when you are comparing current models and prices.
 Should I buy an Apple Watch or a Garmin for my iPhone?
 Buy an Apple Watch if you want a watch that feels like an extension of your iPhone. Setup takes minutes, notifications arrive without fuss, and things such as Apple Pay, calls and apps work in the way you’d expect. For everyday convenience – checking a message on the train, paying for coffee or leaving your phone in your pocket – it’s hard to beat.
 Garmin is the better fit if your watch is primarily a training companion and the thought of another nightly charge makes you groan. The Venu X1 works with iPhone, brings maps, Garmin Coach and Training Readiness, and can last up to nine days with its always-on display off. You sacrifice some of Apple’s polish, but gain the sort of endurance and workout depth keen runners and cyclists will appreciate.
 What is the best budget smartwatch for iPhone users?
 The Amazfit Active 2 is our current best budget smartwatch for iPhone users because it packs in far more than its price suggests. It has a bright AMOLED display, a light, classic-looking design, strong GPS and workout tracking, plus an onboard AI assistant – plenty of useful smartwatch basics, without the usual Apple Watch outlay.
 In our testing, it was comfortable to wear and its calorie and workout figures held their own against an Apple Watch Ultra 2. Amazfit says it can manage five days of heavy use, too, which is a welcome break from daily charging. Want the full watchOS experience and closer iPhone integration? Spend more on the Apple Watch SE 3; the Active 2 is for buyers who want plenty of watch for less.
 Do non-Apple smartwatches work with an iPhone?
 Yes – you are not locked into an Apple Watch just because you own an iPhone. Garmin, Amazfit and Huawei watches can pair through their companion apps, delivering notifications, activity tracking and health or workout data. 
 The catch is that the experience is rarely as joined-up. Third-party watches can be great for fitness and endurance, but app interaction, replying to messages, calls, payments and data syncing may be more limited. Check the companion app supports your iPhone and current iOS version, then make sure the features you actually use are on the list before clicking buy.
 Do Apple Watch health features work in every country?
 No. Apple Watch health features are not a one-size-fits-all deal: availability can vary by country, model, software version and local regulations. ECG, blood oxygen and hypertension notifications are among the features that can differ, so a watch bought in one market may not have exactly the same health toolkit in another.
 If a particular health feature is your reason for buying, check Apple’s current watchOS feature-availability page for your country before handing over your money. And while these tools can be useful for spotting trends or prompting a conversation, they are not a substitute for medical advice – speak to a clinician if you receive an alert or have a concern.

 The best Fitbits were among the first high-quality fitness trackers, an upgrade to the pedometer, when they first launched almost 20 years ago. Since then, the brand's innovations have meant women can track almost every part of their wellbeing from their wrist.
 Now, with Google’s buyout powering smarter features, deeper health insights, and a brand new app for tracking your data, the Fitbit ecosystem feels more advanced than ever.
 I’ve spent the past five years testing the best fitness trackers and smartwatches. This looks out for any irregularities in your heart rate and can be used to potentially flag issues that you can discuss with your doctor.
 It's also great for sleep insights. You can scroll across the touchscreen to view your sleep insights on the Sense 2, making it the best Fitbit for those prioritising learning how to sleep better this year. You can see your overall sleep duration and your sleep score for the night, and with the 6 months of free Fitbit Premium that comes with the device, you can view your Sleep Profile on the device too. Provided you wear the Sense 2 for at least 14 days a month, you'll see your main sleep characteristics on your wrist whenever you like.
 Generally, in testing, I found the Sense 2 smartwatch prioritises complete wellbeing over fitness-specific achievements. Along with improved sleep analysis, there are advanced sensors: blood glucose tracking, an EDA scan app for advanced stress management, and Sp02 blood oxygen level tracking. These are useful for overall health monitoring and great for anyone looking to improve their fitness through better recovery rates, on the lookout for irregular heart rhythms, or monitoring their breathing rate. These are not included in many older versions of the Fitbit, but they do feature on the Fitbit Versa 3 and 4, so it's worth comparing the Fitbit Sense 2 vs Versa 4 before making a final decision.
 Along with all these advanced features, it does the basics very well. I found I could start and navigate through any one of the 40+ workout modes with ease and it's still easy to use with a simple navigation system. The addition of a side button was a welcome return, and there is a dedicated page for the element of fitness tracking most important to you, whether that's steps done, calories burned, distance covered, and so on, so you can prioritise what's important to you.
 Read our full review of the Fitbit Sense 2 here. 
 How I tested the best Fitbits 
 After consulting the experts on important factors to consider, I tested each Fitbit over several weeks through various workouts, from strength training to spin classes, hiking, running, and more daily activities, assessing each model on a range of factors that impact day-to-day use.
 Kate Rowe-Ham , a level 3 qualified personal trainer, specialist women's health coach, and founder of Owning Your Menopause , was one of the professionals I spoke to during testing for many of these watches. She is also a fan of the brand. "These devices allow you to track important benchmarks in your fitness, like your daily step count. Once you can see how you're doing in various areas each day, such as your sleep and activity, you have a clear benchmark to improve on moving forward," she says. "As the saying goes, what gets measured gets managed, and over time, you'll be able to spot any trends that may be affecting your wellbeing."
 When testing the best Fitbits, I considered the following: 
 How easy it was to use: A tracker that charges quickly, has a long-lasting battery life, and is easy to navigate during sweaty workouts is key. It's where screen size and responsivity play a huge role, so I tested to see how easy each of the best Fitbits was to use.
 How comfortable it was to wear: I noted how comfortable each of the smartwatches and trackers was to wear - no one wants a wristband that rubs uncomfortably against the skin or catches on clothing after all.
 The features it offers: There are so many Fitbit models out there now - some people will want a Fitbit that offers features such as contactless payment, on-screen text messages, and music streaming. Others might want a Fitbit that tracks daily activity and sleep patterns, so we've tested a range of the best Fitbits with different features.
 Accuracy of heart-rate monitoring: More advanced models will be able to track in more detail, comparing where your current heart rate sits against your usual maximal heart rate (MHR) to assess how hard you’re working at any given point.
 Waterproofing: Most Fitbit models are swimproof and waterproof to 50m but this is important to consider. "If swimming forms a part of your exercise routine, or even if it's just a recreational activity you enjoy," he says.
 Built-in or smartphone GPS: "Some models include GPS built-in, which is more accurate for tracking distance than devices that use an accelerometer, such as many smartphones."
 I also tested... 
 I've tested many other Fitbit devices over the last five years, including the Fitbit Versa 4 . It's a great Fitbit and was on this list until the release of the Fitbit Edge and Pixel Watch 5. These releases meant the Versa's smartwatch features were no longer progressive or original. I also found the fitness, sleep, and health tracking features on more affordable, newer models.
 I also tested the Fitbit Charge 5 , Versa 3 , Fitbit Luxe, Charge 4 , the Inspire 2, and the Google Pixel Watch 3 . However, either these devices are no longer available to buy online, it's been surpassed by other features on newer models, or it's still available but I'd consider it overpriced for the features in 2026.
 Last year, Google announced that it would no longer produce new versions of the Fitbit Versa or the Fitbit Sense, the brand's original smartwatches, choosing instead to focus on the Pixel line-up.
 Over the years, I've tested older Fitbits and reviewed them for this guide, including the Fitbit Versa 3 and Charge 5. 
 (Image credit: Grace Walsh/Future)
 Are Fitbits waterproof? 
 All of the best Fitbits are water-resistant up to 50 meters. "They're designed to be swim-proof and stand up to even the sweatiest of workouts," the brand says, making them perfect for exploring all the benefits of swimming . However, no Fitbit will be suitable for diving or deeper submersion than this, and the brand warns against wearing the device in any warm environment, like a hot tub or sauna.
 Some Fitbits, such as the Versa 3, have a swim lock so you can go swimming or take the device in the shower without an issue. Having the swim lock enabled isn't essential. It will prevent the water from acting on the touchscreen and navigating around the watch accidentally. Most settings and metrics are controlled via the app, like changing the time on a Fitbit , so you don't have to worry about these being impacted by the water.
 Some straps are also not water-resistant but can withstand sweat. These include:
 Woven straps (Sense and Versa 3)
 Hook and Loop bands (Charge 5)
 Knit bands (Sense and Versa 3)
 If you want a completely water-resistant band, opt for the Infinity band that comes included when you buy one of the best Fitbits, or the Sports band, which is more breathable.
 Fitbit is also keen to emphasise that mishandling the device in particular ways, like dropping it, exposing it to perfumes, including soap and sunscreen, and high-velocity water pressure, will also reduce the waterproof capacity of the device.

 Frequently Asked Questions 
 What's the best smartwatch for women?
 We've got a more detailed entry on this topic below , but in short, for the most part there are no major differences between smartwatches for women and men.
 That said, size may be a favor here, so you may prefer to look for a model that's designed for smaller wrists, such as Garmin's Lily range. 
 Some smartwatches also provide features specific to women's health, although in other cases these are options available within the platform you're using and are not restricted to particular models; Apple Watch Series 8 or later, including the Series 11 and Apple Watch Ultra models...
 How do you charge a smartwatch?
 Unlike smartphones, most smartwatches tend to use a proprietary charger, often a magnetic one. Though they are always included with the watch, this can be frustrating if you lose yours or it breaks. 
 Some chargers will work for multiple models – for instance many Garmins and most Apple Watches are capable of using the same charger, although some older chargers may not be as fast as newer ones. Some can also be charged wirelessly either using Wireless PowerShare from a phone or the Qi standard; check your specific model for details. 
 Which model you use, you should generally remove it from the charger once it’s full; though most devices will have built-in safety features to prevent overcharging, leaving your watch on charge for too long could still degrade the device's lithium-ion battery over time.
 How to set the time on a smartwatch
 Unlike with a non-smart watch, setting the time on a smartwatch is simply a matter of syncing the device to your phone via Bluetooth, using the relevant app. The smartwatch will then take the time from the phone.
 What's the best military smartwatch?
 Several of the best rugged smartwatches are also good choices for military use, and you can also buy plenty of non-smart watches from the likes of Casio that have many useful features for the military including top-notch weatherproofing, long battery life, night-vision backlighting and more. 
 Focusing solely on smart models, Garmin offers a range of ‘Tactical Edition’ watches with ‘stealth’ mode, ballistics information (like a compass/golf watch, that takes wind and weapon range into account) and a quick-wipe ‘kill switch’.
 How does a smartwatch measure sleep?
 Smartwatches are a great way to track the duration and quality of your sleep. Whatever the model, a smartwatch will use heart-rate variability information and motion detection to estimate sleep stages and quality – with varying degrees of accuracy.
 Some smartwatches, such as the Samsung Galaxy Watch 9 and the latest Apple Watch models, including the Series 11 and Ultra 3, even have advanced features such as sleep apnea detection.
 How do you set up a smartwatch?
 How you set up your smartwatch will depend on which model you have, but all will follow a roughly similar process.
 In almost all cases you'll follow instructions to sync the smartwatch to your phone – either by scanning the watch with your phone’s camera if using an Apple Watch, or by downloading an app – and will then follow instructions from there.
 Every smartwatch will have its own app, whether Garmin, Pixel, Apple, Polar, Amazfit or any others.
 How to choose the best smartwatch for you 
 Unfortunately, your choice of smartwatch often depends on your choice of phone, as not all wearables are compatible with competitor devices. Apple Watch only works with Apple iPhones. Samsung and Google watches, and other Wear OS devices, only work with Android devices, but you can use a Samsung watch with a Google phone and vice versa.
 Dedicated fitness watches from Garmin, Coros and Polar generally offer much longer battery life than Wear OS or Apple watches, often lasting a week or more between charges. If training is your priority, they're worth considering even if they don't offer the same app ecosystem.
 Most wearables will get about a day of battery life, which will be disappointing if you're converting from a Garmin watch that lasts weeks. You can find a few watches that last longer on this list.
 Finally, smartwatches can be expensive, and frankly, they don't offer much value for what you pay. Before you spring for an Apple Watch Ultra, you might ask if you are really going Scuba diving this year, or if you're just going to check your text messages without disturbing your dinner mates.
 The best smartwatch for women vs men: Is there a difference?
 There are no specific differences when it comes to smartwatches for women or men, and choosing the right one usually comes down to personal preference. 
 One of the main considerations is making sure the watch size fits your wrist. Many smartwatches are quite large, which can feel bulky on slimmer wrists, so it’s worth checking the case size before buying. Many models come in multiple sizes, and when that’s the case, we list the options in our full reviews to help you choose the best fit.
 Some smartwatches also include features focused on women's health. These can include menstrual cycle tracking, ovulation predictions, and symptom logging, often powered by data such as heart rate trends, sleep patterns, and skin temperature. These tools can help provide a broader picture of hormonal cycles and overall well-being.
 This doesn't mean those watches are only designed for women, nor that these features must be used. Most are optional and can be enabled or ignored depending on your preferences.
 If you do plan to use them, it's worth checking the privacy policy of the watch you've bought so you understand where your health data is stored and who can access it.
 Can you use Apple Watch with an Android phone?
 The first thing to check is whether your phone is compatible with the smartwatch you want. You can't use an Apple Watch with an Android phone, as all the functions of watchOS require iOS to interface with. 
 You can't use an Apple Watch with an Android phone, as Apple Watch requires an iPhone for setup and everyday use.
 Likewise, Google Pixel Watch and Samsung Galaxy Watch models are designed for Android phones and don't support iPhone. If you regularly switch between Android and iOS, a Garmin, Amazfit or CMF smartwatch is usually a better choice because these work with both platforms.
 How we test smartwatches 
 Every smartwatch on this list has been fully and extensively reviewed by the expert team at TechRadar, so we know exactly what makes them tick.
 Our review process involves using the devices as if they were our own personal wearables, ensuring every smartwatch gets fully tested in the real world. A comprehensive sweep of features takes place, and usage is varied over a week to give us a clear idea of how battery life performs.
 When testing in-house, we generally look at how accurate the GPS is on each smartwatch by testing it against an industry leader such as the Garmin Epix Pro . Likewise for workout metrics. We also rank how usable the watch's operating system is, whether it supports third-party apps, and where it sits in the market. For example, a cheap watch with fewer features is more likely to get four stars than a feature-stuffed premium watch that isn't worth the expensive price.
 Using that knowledge we've then ranked them, factoring in their value, design, features, and performance to get an overall star verdict.

Best watches for HYROX (2026): training vs race day 
 Race day 15 min read Best fitness trackers and watches for HYROX (2026): training vs race day
 Which watches work indoors with no GPS: HYROX race modes by brand, wrist vs chest-strap heart rate, footpods, and picks for training and race day.
 By Tim Grassin , founder of RoxSkin · Last checked October 20, 2026 · 32 sources 
 The best HYROX watch is one that makes lap-taking easy indoors, paired with a chest strap if you care about heart rate. HYROX is raced inside with no usable GPS, the official splits come from the timing chip on your ankle, and wrist heart rate struggles at the sleds, carries and wall balls. So the right device for training (load, recovery, heart-rate zones) isn't always the right one for race day (big buttons, a simple screen, a reliable race mode). This guide compares the race modes that actually exist as of October 2026, explains the indoor accuracy problems, and gives picks by budget and athlete type.

 Note
 We're not affiliated with any watch brand and haven't lab-tested these devices. Features and prices are as checked on 20 October 2026 and change with firmware updates, so check before you buy. 
 The short answer: our picks
 COROS PACE 4 + a chest strap
 Best overall Around $249

 Best for race day Around $370

 Best for training and recovery Around $550 / $750 
 Deepest training-load, readiness and HRV tools; HYROX via multisport set-ups or Connect IQ apps.
 Amazfit Active 2
 Best budget Around $100 
 Listed with HYROX race mode at a low price, but behind on new features.
 Keep your Apple Watch
 You already own an Apple Watch Add a HYROX app and a chest strap 
 No native HYROX workout, but third-party apps and Bluetooth straps fill most of the gap.
 Polar H10 chest strap
 Best single upgrade for any watch Around $105 
 Far more reliable heart rate than any wrist sensor at the stations.
 Key takeaway
 Do you even need one? No. You can finish, and race well, without a watch. Your official run, station and Roxzone splits come from the chip timing and appear in your results afterwards. A watch earns its place in training, where heart-rate zones and load help you pace and recover, and on race day only if it helps you stick to a plan without thinking.
 Why HYROX is hard for wearables
 Most sports watches are built for outdoor endurance: GPS for distance, a steady rhythm for the optical heart-rate sensor, one sport at a time. HYROX breaks all three.
 No GPS indoors, so run distance is a guess
 HYROX runs in halls and arenas, where GPS signal is weak or bounces off the roof. Turn GPS off. Without it, your watch estimates distance from your wrist movement (the accelerometer), and that estimate drifts with tight laps, turns, crowds and a tired, shorter stride. It may say you ran 7.2 km or 8.9 km. Neither number matters: the course is measured by the organisers, and you run the laps you're told to run.
 Tip
 Use lap time , not distance, to judge your runs. If you want a live indoor pace number, a footpod such as Stryd is far more consistent than the wrist, because it measures your foot directly.
 A footpod measures your foot directly, so indoor pace and distance stay consistent where wrist estimates drift. 
 Sixteen segments plus the Roxzone
 A race is 8 runs and 8 stations, with the Roxzone transition area in between. That's at least 16 segments, and more if you want transitions timed separately. Every segment change is a button press, unless your watch's race mode detects it for you. Under fatigue, people forget presses, press twice, or knock the crown with a wrist bend. One reviewer testing the Amazfit Balance 3 found forgetting to press at transitions the biggest usability problem in simulations.
 Wrist heart rate struggles at the stations
 Optical (PPG) sensors shine light into your wrist and read blood flow. They work best when the wrist is still and the rhythm is steady, like easy running. HYROX stations do the opposite:
 Sled push and pull, farmers carry: a hard grip and flexed wrist tighten the tendons under the sensor and change blood flow.
 Wall balls, burpee broad jumps, SkiErg: repeated impacts and arm swings shift the watch on your skin.
 Sweat loosens the seal between sensor and skin.
 A hard grip and a flexed wrist at the sled change blood flow under the sensor, so wrist heart rate is least reliable here. 
 The research agrees. A Cleveland Clinic study (Gillinov et al., 2017) found a chest strap matched ECG best, and optical wrist devices varied by exercise type. A 2020 study in npj Digital Medicine (Bent et al.) found optical error was around 30% higher during activity than at rest. A small 2025 study of wrist-worn Garmin watches during deadlifts found error grew at higher intensity and recommended a chest strap for resistance training. Hands-on testers report the same pattern in HYROX simulations, with wrist readings spiking or lagging in the hardest efforts.

 A chest strap reads heart rate from the heart's electrical signal, which is why it stays accurate at the stations. Wet the electrodes and tighten it a notch more than for running. 
 Knocks and buttons
 The sled handles, kettlebells and wall ball can all hit your watch. Some people wear it a little further up the forearm, or on the non-dominant wrist. Physical buttons beat touchscreens with sweaty fingers, and a button lock stops accidental pauses.
 Which brands have a HYROX or hybrid race mode? (October 2026)
 Only two big watch brands have a built-in mode designed for this format. Everyone else relies on multisport set-ups or third-party apps.
 Amazfit: the official HYROX mode
 Amazfit (Zepp Health) became HYROX's official wearable and timekeeping partner in August 2024, and in April 2026 signed a three-year global deal. It's the only brand that can call its mode "HYROX".
 What it has: a HYROX Race Mode (Single, Doubles or Relay), race simulations, a training library, Virtual Pace against a plan you build in the Zepp app, and post-race analysis with heart rate per station. Amazfit says a Stryd footpod can provide indoor run pace in Race Mode.
 Segment handling: reviewers describe pressing a button to move between runs and stations. Amazfit's own roadmap, reported by the5krunner in September 2026, schedules automatic transitions for flagship watches (including Balance 3, Active 3 Premium, T-Rex 3 and Cheetah 2 Pro) from October 2026, with Balance 2 and Active Max following in November. Roadmaps slip, so check your watch's release notes before relying on it.
 Models: Amazfit's HYROX page lists race mode on the Balance Ultra, 3 and 2, T-Rex Ultra 2, 3 Pro and 3, Cheetah 2 Pro and Ultra, Active Max, Active 3 Premium, Active 2, Bip Max and Bip 6. Older and cheaper models get fewer of the newest features.
 Helio Strap Pro: an optional upper-arm band Amazfit says adds station movement tracking and continuous arm heart rate. It needs a compatible Amazfit watch. Early reviews are cautious about how useful the extra data is.
 COROS: Hybrid Fitness mode
 COROS added a mode called Hybrid Fitness in its March 2026 update. It covers the same eight stations in the standard order, with Race, Training and Test modes.
 Segment handling: COROS says the watch can auto-detect when you move between a run and a station, or you can switch to manual transitions with the Back/Lap button. Race options include individual, doubles and relay.
 Models: PACE 4, PACE 3, PACE Pro, APEX 4, APEX 2 and 2 Pro, NOMAD, VERTIX 2 and 2S. Older models (PACE 2, APEX Pro, VERTIX 1) don't get it.
 Footpods: COROS watches pair with Stryd for indoor pace.
 Caveats: in an early test of the Test mode on an APEX 2 Pro, a reviewer pressed to change legs, still saw some per-leg times recorded wrongly, and got no rep counts. Test it in a full simulation before race day.
 Garmin: no native mode, but lots of workarounds
 As of October 2026 Garmin has no HYROX activity profile. You have three good options:
 Repeat multisport: build a two-leg profile (an indoor run with GPS off, then Cardio) and set it to repeat, with auto-lap and transitions off. Garmin's own Swedish blog describes a similar Lap-button set-up. Each segment saves separately.
 Cardio with laps: copy the Cardio profile, turn GPS off, show lap time, total time and heart rate, and press Lap at each change. Simple, one activity, no station names.
 Connect IQ apps: free and paid third-party apps (for example Hyrox Tracker, ROXZONE, RoxTrack, Hybrid Smash) add station names, 16-split recording and, in some, Roxzone timing. They're independent of HYROX and Garmin, so check compatibility and reviews.
 Garmin's real strength is training: Training Readiness, HRV Status, Training Load and Acute Load, recovery time, a strength activity with rep counting, and support for chest straps and footpods. The HRM 600 strap also stores heart rate if the connection drops.
 Apple Watch: apps do the work
 The Workout app has no HYROX workout. Options:
 Third-party apps on the App Store, such as HyRhythm, RoxWatch and others, track runs, stations and transitions, often with current and next station on screen. Quality varies, and they're independent of HYROX.
 A built-in workout with manual segments: some athletes use one workout and mark segments as they go. It's workable, but you'll get less useful data.
 Pair a Bluetooth chest strap. Apple Watch supports Bluetooth heart-rate sensors, which fixes the biggest weakness.
 Battery is the other limit: the regular Series lasts about a day, which is fine for a race but means charging habits matter in race week. The Ultra lasts considerably longer.
 Polar, Suunto and Samsung
 None has an official HYROX mode that we could find. Polar watches (Vantage V3, Grit X2) can use a custom sport profile or multisport set-up with manual laps, and Polar's H10 strap is the reference sensor in many accuracy studies. Suunto users build a custom sport mode with lap number, lap time, heart rate and total time on one screen. Samsung Galaxy Watch reviewers describe a custom multi-sport workout with manual laps. All three support external heart-rate straps.
 WHOOP and Oura: training only
 Screenless trackers can't take laps or show you anything mid-race, so they're training and recovery tools.
 WHOOP (memberships from around $149 a year) tracks strain, recovery, HRV and sleep, and its Strength Trainer feature adds muscular load from logged sets. One long-term tester found its wrist heart rate unreliable in HYROX simulations but accurate when worn on the upper arm in a sleeve. It can broadcast heart rate to a watch or gym equipment.
 Oura (Ring 4 from around $349, plus a membership of about $6 a month in the US) is strong on sleep and readiness. A ring takes a beating under kettlebell handles and sled grips, so many people take it off for heavy grip work.

 Training with a tracker: what actually matters
 Your watch is most useful in the 12 to 16 weeks before a race, not on race day.
 Heart-rate zones
 Most HYROX training is aerobic base work plus threshold intervals, and heart rate is the easiest way to keep easy days easy. Set your zones from a recent test (lactate threshold or a max-effort field test) rather than an age formula. Our VO2max calculator gives you a baseline and an 8-week plan, and how to train for HYROX explains how zones fit a weekly structure.
 Training load and readiness
 Garmin, COROS, Polar, Amazfit and WHOOP all estimate training load and recovery. They're helpful for spotting trends, like a run of red days or a load spike after you add a second sled session. Treat them as prompts, not orders. Heart-rate-based load under-counts heavy strength work, because a sled push is hard on muscles without raising heart rate for long.
 Strength tracking
 Automatic rep counting is unreliable for HYROX moves like sled pushes, lunges and burpee broad jumps. Log sets and loads yourself, or use a strength feature where you enter them (WHOOP's Strength Trainer, Garmin's strength activity). What matters is progressive overload over weeks, not the watch's rep count.
 Treadmill and indoor running
 Calibrate: Garmin lets you correct treadmill distance at the end of a run. Apple Watch improves its indoor estimate from outdoor GPS runs.
 Footpods: Stryd (around $300 for one pod; check current pricing) gives consistent indoor pace and distance on most major watches, and a reviewer found it within a few seconds per mile of the treadmill display. It's a training luxury, not a requirement.
 Lap time over pace: In compromised-running sessions (run, station, run), log lap times for each 1 km and compare them over weeks.
 Pacing by heart rate and effort
 On race day you'll pace by lap time, breathing and perceived effort (RPE), with heart rate as a check on the runs. Practise that in training: run 1 km after a sled or wall-ball set, note your time and how hard it felt, and learn what "sustainable" feels like with tired legs. Plan your target splits with the HYROX pace calculator , then read HYROX pacing and the Roxzone for how to spread the effort.
 Screenless trackers: pros and cons
 Pros
 Comfortable 24/7.
 Strong sleep and HRV data.
 Nothing to knock at the stations.
 WHOOP can sit on your upper arm.
 Cons
 No laps.
 No live data.
 No race mode.
 Monthly fees.
 A common set-up is a screenless tracker for recovery plus a simple watch or chest strap for sessions.
 Race-day set-up checklist
 Watch out
 First, the rules. The 26/27 rulebook's list of permitted items doesn't include watches, and items that aren't listed are treated as not allowed by default. The official wearable partner sells a race mode, but judges follow the rulebook, so check your event's athlete guide or ask customer service before race day. See what's not allowed at HYROX for the rest.
 If you do race with a watch:
 Build the race in advance. Use your watch's HYROX or Hybrid Fitness mode, a Connect IQ or App Store app, or a repeat multisport profile. Set it for 16 segments, or about 32 if you time each Roxzone entry and exit separately.
 Do one full or half simulation with that exact set-up at least two weeks before the race, including the button presses.
 Turn GPS and auto-lap off. They'll only give you wrong splits.
 Lock the buttons or touchscreen if your watch allows it, so a wall-ball squat doesn't pause your recording.
 Fit the strap properly. Wet the chest strap electrodes, tighten it a notch more than for running, and check it's paired before you enter the start pen.
 Charge everything the night before , including the strap if it's rechargeable.
 Keep the screen simple: total time, lap time and heart rate, in large digits. Station names are nice but not needed.
 Don't trust distance or indoor pace unless you're using a footpod.
 Afterwards, use the official results for your true splits, and your watch for heart rate by segment.
 Our race-day planner builds a race-morning timeline and checklist, and the packing list covers everything else.
 What to show on the watch face
 Main screen: lap time (biggest), total time, heart rate.
 Optional second screen: a target split for the current segment, or time of day, if your app supports a race plan.
 Leave off: distance, pace without a footpod, cadence and anything you have to scroll to.
 Common race-day mistakes
 Chasing heart rate at the stations. Wrist heart rate is least reliable there. Pace stations by effort and breathing.
 Forgetting or doubling a lap press, then spending a run trying to fix it. Leave it and keep racing.
 Pacing runs by the watch's distance. It's wrong indoors. Use lap time.
 Trying a new app or mode on race day. If you haven't simulated with it, don't race with it.
 Getting distracted by data. If checking the watch costs you focus, race by feel and review the numbers later.
 Recommendations by athlete type and budget
 First-timer, any budget: use what you have, or nothing. If you buy one thing, make it a chest strap for training. Learn pacing by effort first.
 Budget under about $150: Amazfit Active 2 for a built-in HYROX mode, or keep your current watch and add a Polar H10.
 Mid-range ($250 to $400): COROS PACE 4 or Amazfit Balance 3, both with built-in race modes and Stryd support. Add a chest strap if heart rate matters to you.
 Data-driven trainer: Garmin Forerunner 570 or 970 with an HRM 600 or H10 and a Connect IQ HYROX app. Add Stryd if you train on treadmills.
 iPhone user: keep or buy an Apple Watch (Series 12 or Ultra 4 for longer battery), add a third-party HYROX app and a Bluetooth chest strap.
 Recovery-focused or wears a ring already: WHOOP (worn on the upper arm in sessions) or Oura for sleep and readiness, plus a cheap watch or strap for workouts.
 Pro division or chasing a big PB: the watch matters less than the plan. Use it in training to keep easy work easy and threshold work honest, then race by lap time. See how to improve your HYROX time .
 FAQ
 What is the best watch for HYROX?
 There's no single best watch, because training and racing need different things. For value, the COROS PACE 4 has a built-in Hybrid Fitness race mode and good training tools. For a dedicated race mode, Amazfit (the official HYROX wearable partner) has the most complete HYROX features, such as on the Balance 3. For training and recovery data, Garmin's Forerunner range is the most thorough. Pair any of them with a chest strap for reliable heart rate.
 Does Garmin have a HYROX mode?
 Not as of October 2026. Garmin users set up a repeating multisport profile (indoor run plus Cardio), use a Cardio activity with manual laps, or install a third-party Connect IQ app that records runs, stations and sometimes Roxzone times. Check app compatibility for your model.
 Does Apple Watch have a HYROX workout?
 No, the Workout app has no HYROX workout. Third-party App Store apps track runs, stations and transitions, and you can pair a Bluetooth chest strap for better heart rate at the stations.
 Can you wear a watch during a HYROX race?
 The 26/27 rulebook's permitted list doesn't include watches, and unlisted items are prohibited by default. Check your event's athlete guide or ask customer service before race day, rather than finding out at the start line.
 Is wrist heart rate accurate during HYROX?
 It's reasonable on the runs and ergs, but often wrong at the sled push, sled pull, farmers carry and wall balls, where grip, wrist flexion and impact disturb the optical sensor. A chest strap is the most accurate option, and an upper-arm optical band is a good second choice.
 Why is my watch's run distance wrong at HYROX?
 Because there's no reliable GPS indoors, so the watch estimates distance from your arm movement. Tight laps, turns and tired running throw the estimate off. The course is measured for you, so pace by lap time, or use a footpod like Stryd for consistent indoor pace.
 Do I need a footpod for HYROX?
 No. A footpod gives more consistent pace and distance indoors and on treadmills, which helps in training. On race day, lap times and effort work fine, and your official splits come from chip timing.
 Is WHOOP or Oura good for HYROX training?
 Yes, for recovery, sleep and training load, but not for racing, because they have no screen or lap button. WHOOP's heart rate is more accurate on the upper arm than the wrist during HYROX-style sessions. Many people pair a screenless tracker with a watch or chest strap for workouts.

 What Makes the Best Watch for HYROX? 
 Most running watches track well on a flat road. HYROX is not a flat road. You’re transitioning between 8 km of running and 8 functional stations inside an exhibition hall — and the best watch for HYROX needs to keep up with all of it. Here’s what separates a genuinely useful HYROX watch from one that becomes dead weight on your wrist.
 GPS and Indoor Tracking 
 HYROX races happen indoors, which is the enemy of GPS accuracy. The 1 km running loops run inside convention centers and exhibition halls with heavy metal infrastructure. A watch that relies solely on satellite signal will show wildly inaccurate distances — making any pace data essentially useless.
 The best watch for HYROX offers an accelerometer-based indoor running mode or foot pod compatibility (such as Stryd). Amazfit’s dedicated HYROX mode handles indoor tracking natively — a real advantage over most competitors on this list.
 Heart Rate Accuracy Under Load 
 During sled pushes and burpee broad jumps, your wrist position shifts constantly. Optical wrist HR sensors struggle under these conditions. The best watch for HYROX either has an exceptionally stable HR sensor or supports Bluetooth chest strap pairing for accurate zone data across every station.
 💡 
 Info 
 Pairing any watch with a chest strap (like the Garmin HRM-Pro or Polar H10) dramatically improves heart rate accuracy during functional stations. If you’re serious about pacing by zone, this $60–$80 accessory matters more than upgrading your watch model.
 Durability and Button Control 
 Touchscreens and sweat don’t mix. During a 1,000m row or a set of wall balls, you need to lap your watch with a single button press — without looking down for more than half a second. Every option in our best watch for HYROX list has physical buttons for exactly this reason.
 Durability matters too. Sled push grip pressure and sandbag lunges put real stress on watch bezels. Gorilla Glass or sapphire crystal lenses are worth the premium if you race more than once a year. If your legs take the same beating during those stations, a compression leg sleeve for HYROX is worth the same consideration as your watch bezel.
 Battery Life 
 A HYROX race lasts between 60 and 180 minutes depending on your level. Race-day battery survival is never the real question. What matters is whether your watch handles 3–4 weeks of daily training without stress. Every best watch for HYROX pick on this list survives race day comfortably — battery life differentiates training comfort, not race survival.
 The 7 Best Watches for HYROX in 2026 
 Every watch below was selected on four criteria: indoor tracking quality, HR accuracy under functional load, physical usability during stations, and value for money at its price point. These are the best watch for HYROX options available right now.
 1. Amazfit Cheetah Pro — Best Overall Watch for HYROX 
 Price range: ~$220–$250 
 If you want the single best watch for HYROX without spending Fenix money, this is it. Amazfit is the official global wearable partner of HYROX — and the Cheetah Pro is the only watch with a dedicated built-in HYROX Race Mode that tracks all 8 stations, the running segments, and transitions in one structured workout. No manual mode switching between the SkiErg and the run — the watch manages it automatically.
 The Cheetah Pro uses dual-band GPS with BioTracker 4.0 optical HR. For indoor running accuracy, it supports Stryd foot pod integration — solving the GPS drift problem every other watch faces inside a convention center. The AMOLED display stays readable under sweat, and the physical crown button gives you reliable lap control mid-station. As the best watch for HYROX at its price point, the Cheetah Pro offers functionality no competitor matches below $400.
 ✅ 
 Best For 
 Athletes who want a purpose-built HYROX experience without paying premium prices. The dedicated race mode alone saves significant setup time and gives you cleaner post-race splits than any manually configured multisport profile.
 2. Garmin Forerunner 265 — Best Watch for HYROX Running-Focused Athletes 
 Price range: ~$350–$400 
 For athletes whose HYROX race lives or dies by running pace — and for most people it does — the Forerunner 265 is the best watch for HYROX in the mid-range Garmin lineup. At approximately 47g, it’s the lightest watch on this list, which means zero arm swing interference during running segments. The AMOLED screen performs excellently in low-light indoor venues.
 Garmin added a HYROX Activity Profile via firmware update, letting you track race segments with more structure than a generic multisport mode. Training load analysis, VO2 Max tracking, and race predictor tools make this the strongest daily training companion on the list. It’s not as plug-and-play as the Amazfit for race day, but for the 12 weeks of training before the gun goes off, nothing matches it at this price.
 Pair the data this watch generates with a structured training block. Our complete HYROX training guide shows exactly how to use pace and HR data to structure your build-up.
 3. Garmin Fenix 8 (47mm) — Best Premium Watch for HYROX 
 Price range: ~$700–$900 
 The Fenix 8 is overkill for most HYROX athletes — but if you also run ultras or triathlons, it’s the most complete tool on the market. As the best watch for HYROX at the premium end, the sapphire crystal lens, titanium casing, and MIL-STD-810 durability rating mean it handles every station with zero damage risk. Dual-frequency multi-band GPS delivers the best indoor/outdoor tracking available in any consumer watch.
 In practice, the Fenix 8 gives you ecosystem depth and longevity rather than HYROX-specific features the Forerunner 265 can’t already match. Only consider it if you’re a confirmed multi-sport athlete who wants one watch for the next decade.
 4. Coros Pace 3 — Best Budget Watch for HYROX 
 Price range: ~$200–$230 
 At under $230, the Coros Pace 3 is the best budget watch for HYROX on the market. Dual-frequency GPS, a multisport mode, and one of the best battery lives in its class — up to 17 days smartwatch mode, 38 hours GPS mode — make it a standout value for athletes entering their first race without wanting to overspend on gear.
 The dial-style physical button is one of the most reliable lap controls available — no accidental screen presses during the farmers carry or wall balls. What it lacks is a native HYROX mode and the analytical depth of Garmin’s platform. You’ll need to configure a custom multisport profile manually once, which takes about 10 minutes and works seamlessly on race day. For pure cost-per-feature value, nothing beats it as a best watch for HYROX entry point.
 ⚠️ 
 Warning 
 The Coros Pace 3 comes with a nylon band as standard. It’s comfortable for training but absorbs sweat heavily during a full HYROX race. Pick up a spare silicone strap before race day — widely available for under $15.
 5. Apple Watch Ultra 3 — Best Watch for HYROX Apple Ecosystem Users 
 Price range: ~$800–$900 
 If your entire life runs through an iPhone, the Apple Watch Ultra 3 is a capable best watch for HYROX option — though not for purely sport-specific reasons. The Action Button delivers one-press lap control with wet hands, the titanium case is the most impact-resistant on this list, and up to 36 hours battery in low-power mode is a real step forward over older Apple Watch generations.
 The core limitation is indoor GPS. Apple Watch relies heavily on satellite signal, which degrades significantly inside large metal exhibition halls. Third-party apps like ROXFIT or Runna improve the training experience considerably. If you’re buying a best watch for HYROX from scratch with no existing ecosystem, a Garmin or Amazfit will serve you better at the same or lower price.
 6. Polar Pacer Pro — Best Watch for HYROX Recovery Tracking 
 Price range: ~$280–$320 
 HYROX training is high-volume and high-intensity. The biggest mistake most intermediate athletes make isn’t under-training — it’s failing to recover properly between sessions. As the best watch for HYROX when recovery management is your priority, the Polar Pacer Pro addresses this better than anything else at its price, with detailed HRV tracking, sleep quality scoring, and training load warnings that genuinely change behavior.
 The optical HR sensor is among the most accurate available for wrist-based tracking. GPS is precise outdoors and the watch runs on physical buttons throughout. Its main limitations are average indoor tracking and no native HYROX mode. But for athletes who overtrain or struggle with recovery windows between race-pace sessions, this is the smartest best watch for HYROX choice on this list.
 7. Garmin Forerunner 165 — Best Entry-Level Watch for HYROX 
 Price range: ~$200–$250 
 The Forerunner 165 is the most affordable Garmin with an AMOLED display and solid GPS tracking. It lacks the advanced training load metrics of the 265, and the HR sensor is slightly less accurate under high-intensity station work — but as the best entry-level watch for HYROX, it covers every essential: GPS, lap tracking, heart rate zones, and a battery that lasts well beyond your training week.
 If you’re on your first HYROX race prep and haven’t committed to a premium watch yet, the 165 is the cleanest entry point in the Garmin lineup. Use it to understand which features you actually need in training — that knowledge will drive a smarter upgrade decision later.

 Which Best Watch for HYROX Suits Your Profile? 
 The best watch for HYROX depends less on raw specs and more on where you are in your athlete journey. Here’s a direct breakdown by profile so you can make the right call without overthinking it.
 If You’re a Beginner 
 The best watch for HYROX at beginner level is either the Garmin Forerunner 165 or the Coros Pace 3 . Both cost under $230, both track everything you need for your first race, and neither will overwhelm you with data you can’t yet interpret. Focus on finishing your first event, then decide on an upgrade. Read our guide on what no one tells you before your first HYROX race to understand what else to prepare.
 If You’re Intermediate and Racing Seriously 
 The best watch for HYROX at the intermediate level is the Amazfit Cheetah Pro — it delivers purpose-built HYROX tracking at a price no Garmin can match. If running analysis matters more than a native race mode, the Garmin Forerunner 265 is worth the extra $150 and remains the best watch for HYROX in the Garmin mid-range lineup.
 If Budget Is the Priority 
 The best watch for HYROX on a tight budget is the Coros Pace 3 — no contest. Set up a custom multisport profile once before race day and you have everything you need for under $230. Don’t let gear purchasing delay your actual training. More time running and doing station work will improve your finish time far more than any watch feature.
 If you train across several disciplines beyond HYROX, HybridPace has a roundup of the best fitness trackers for hybrid athletes .
 🚨 
 Important 
 No best watch for HYROX fixes a bad pacing strategy. Going out too fast on runs 1–3 and blowing up from station 5 onward is the most common race-day mistake. Your watch only helps if your strategy is right behind it. See our HYROX running pace guide before race day.
 Common Mistakes When Choosing the Best Watch for HYROX 
 Most athletes overthink the best watch for HYROX decision — or make it for the wrong reasons. Here are the five most common errors to avoid.
 Buying based on brand alone. Garmin is excellent, but an Amazfit with a native HYROX mode gives you better race-day data than a Garmin without one properly configured.
 Ignoring indoor GPS limitations. Most standard GPS watches drift indoors. If your race is inside a metal exhibition hall, a foot pod or dedicated indoor mode isn’t optional — it’s essential for clean splits.
 Prioritizing touchscreen over buttons. Touchscreens are fine for navigating menus. During wall balls or a sled push, they’re a liability. The best watch for HYROX always has physical lap and start/stop buttons.
 Forgetting to charge before race day. This sounds obvious. It happens more than you’d think. Build a pre-race checklist that includes watch charge status. Our full HYROX gear guide covers complete race day prep.
 Spending premium budget on a watch instead of race experience. A $900 watch won’t improve your station times. Train more. Race more. Upgrade when you know exactly what data you’re missing.
 Quick Action Plan: Set Up Your Best Watch for HYROX 
 Once you’ve chosen the best watch for HYROX that fits your budget and profile, here’s how to configure it properly before race day — whether you have a dedicated HYROX mode or need to build a custom multisport profile from scratch.
 Activate or create your HYROX profile. If your watch has a native HYROX mode (Amazfit), activate it directly. If not, build a custom multisport profile: Run → Transition → Functional Workout, repeating 8 times.
 Set auto-lap to 1 km. This gives you automatic splits on every running segment and tells you exactly where you stand against your target pace after each loop.
 Configure heart rate zone alerts. Set a high HR ceiling alert — typically top of Zone 4 — so your watch warns you before you redline on the early running segments.
 Test your setup indoors before race day. Run a full station simulation in your gym with your watch active. Verify that lap control works with wet hands and that HR readings stay stable during sled-style movements.
 Pair a chest strap if HR precision matters. A Bluetooth HR chest strap paired with the best watch for HYROX you choose is a $60–$80 upgrade that outperforms any optical wrist sensor during functional work.
 Charge to 100% the night before. Set a phone reminder. No exceptions, no “it’s probably fine.”
 Simplify your data fields for race day. Display only: current HR, lap time, current pace, total elapsed time. Less scrolling, more racing.
 Don’t let gear decisions delay your race entry. If you haven’t secured your spot yet, use HYTRACK to get instant alerts when HYROX tickets go on sale in your city — before events sell out.
 For official race formats, station requirements, and division rules, refer to the official HYROX website .
 FAQ — Best Watch for HYROX 
 Do I need a special watch for HYROX? 
 You don’t need a specialist watch to compete in HYROX — any GPS watch with heart rate tracking will let you race. However, the best watch for HYROX will have physical buttons, reliable indoor tracking, and a multisport or dedicated race mode that gives you significantly more useful data. The Amazfit Cheetah Pro is currently the only option with a fully native HYROX race mode built in.
 Is the Amazfit really the best watch for HYROX? 
 Amazfit is the official global wearable partner of HYROX, and the Cheetah Pro’s dedicated race mode gives it a clear race-day advantage. For pure running analysis and long-term training load management, Garmin’s ecosystem remains deeper. The best watch for HYROX ultimately depends on whether you prioritize race-day simplicity (Amazfit) or training data depth (Garmin Forerunner 265).
 Can I use an Apple Watch for HYROX? 
 Yes. The Apple Watch Ultra 3 is capable for HYROX, especially for athletes already in the Apple ecosystem. Its main limitations are indoor GPS accuracy and the absence of a native HYROX mode. Third-party apps like ROXFIT help significantly. But if you’re choosing the best watch for HYROX from scratch, a Garmin or Amazfit will serve you better at the same or lower price point.
 What is the best Garmin watch for HYROX? 
 The Garmin Forerunner 265 is the best Garmin watch for HYROX at the mid-range price point. It’s lightweight, features an AMOLED display, supports a HYROX activity profile via firmware update, and provides excellent training load analytics. If budget is open and you’re a multi-sport athlete, the Fenix 8 is the most complete Garmin available — though heavier and significantly more expensive.
 Does a watch actually improve HYROX performance? 
 Indirectly, yes. The best watch for HYROX gives you real-time pacing data that prevents going out too fast — the single most common mistake in the race. Heart rate zone alerts stop you from redlining before station 4. Post-race splits help you identify where you’re losing the most time. None of that makes you fitter, but it makes you smarter. See our guide on where most athletes lose time in HYROX to understand which stations to target.
 What is the best budget watch for HYROX? 
 The Coros Pace 3 at ~$210 is the best budget watch for HYROX. Dual-frequency GPS, a reliable physical dial button, multisport mode, and exceptional battery life make it exceptional value. You’ll need to manually configure a custom HYROX multisport profile — about 10 minutes of setup — and it works cleanly on race day. For new athletes, it covers every essential without overspending on features you won’t use for months.

 Key takeaways
 HYROX runs are indoors, so GPS pace and distance are unreliable. Race on lap time, not distance.
 Amazfit's Balance 3 has a dedicated HYROX race mode and training library. the5krunner rated it 89% but noted average GPS and a large 51.4 mm case.
 Garmin has no built-in HYROX mode in the setup guides we found. You build one with a lap-based profile, a custom workout or the ROXFIT app.
 A footpod such as STRYD (about $200) gives the most accurate indoor run pace.
 The best HYROX watch is not the one with the best GPS. All eight runs are indoors, where satellites barely reach, so the features that win are a reliable lap button, a readable screen and good heart-rate data.
 This guide is based on published reviews and setup guides, listed under Sources. We have not tested these watches ourselves.
 What actually matters
 Lap time over distance. the5krunner advises turning GPS off for the race and using lap time, not distance, to judge each run, because indoor distance is unreliable.
 A footpod for real indoor pace. The same guide suggests a footpod such as STRYD, about $200 , if you want accurate pace on the runs.
 A lap button you trust. You press it at every station exit, so a setup that lets you fix a double press is worth having.
 Fit and size. Sundried recommends a snug strap for better heart-rate readings and a low-profile case that stays out of the way on burpees and sled pulls.
 Pair the watch with your target splits from our free pace band generator and you can check each lap against plan.
 Amazfit Balance 3: the most HYROX features
 the5krunner calls the Balance 3 “the best and most featured HYROX watch you can buy today” and scored it 89% .
 HYROX features: a race mode for the 8 stations and 1 km runs, a PFT benchmark, a HYROX training library, virtual pacing, and singles, doubles and relay formats.
 Price: £369.90 in stainless steel and £449.90 in titanium in the UK. Galaxus listed the Balance 3 and Balance Ultra at about 370 to 600 euros.
 Battery: Amazfit claims up to 21 days and 41 hours of GPS. The reviewer estimated 7 to 10 days with real use.
 Drawbacks: GPS accuracy was average in testing, there were heart-rate dropouts on some outdoor runs, the 51.4 mm case is large for small wrists, and its app store is far smaller than Garmin’s.
 One caveat: the reviewer did not test the race mode’s automatic station detection and pressed the button manually in simulations.
 Sources disagree on the partnership. the5krunner’s Garmin guide calls Amazfit the official HYROX partner, while Galaxus said the partnership was not confirmed.

 Garmin: the biggest ecosystem, some setup required
 Garmin offers about 4,000 apps to Amazfit’s roughly 500, according to the5krunner. The trade-off is setup. Its guide describes four ways to race HYROX on a Garmin:
 Cardio profile, GPS off: press lap at each station exit. The simplest option.
 Repeating multisport profile: an indoor run profile and a station profile that alternate. The author recommends it for higher-end watches such as the Forerunner 970 and Fenix.
 Custom workout: eight run and station repeats built in Garmin Connect. This works on cheaper Garmins, but a wrong press can knock it out of sync.
 ROXFIT app: a HYROX app on Connect IQ with about 50,000 downloads.
 Garmin updates its watches often, so check for newer HYROX support before you build a profile.

 Coros Pace 3: the light budget pick
 Sundried names the Coros Pace 3 as a lightweight, budget-friendly alternative to the Garmin Fenix. the5krunner notes Coros has only limited HYROX multisport support , so expect the simple lap-button approach.
 Check price on Amazon: Coros Pace 3

 You want HYROX features out of the box: Amazfit Balance 3.
 You already train on Garmin or want the most apps: stay with Garmin and set up a lap profile.
 You want light and cheaper: Coros Pace 3 with a basic lap setup.
 Whichever you choose, practise the lap button in a race simulation first. Our pacing guide has split targets for every finish time.

 A GPS watch is one of the most useful tools you can have for HYROX — it lets you pace your 1km runs precisely, monitor your heart rate, and track your station times. This guide covers the best options for HYROX athletes at every budget.
 Why a GPS Watch Matters for HYROX
 Pacing is the most critical skill in HYROX. Going out too fast in the first 2km is the most common reason athletes blow up. A GPS watch showing your real-time 1km pace is the single most effective tool for keeping you honest early in the race.
 What you need from a HYROX watch:
 GPS accuracy — for 1km lap alerts and pace tracking indoors
 Heart rate monitoring — to manage effort across 8 runs and 8 stations
 Auto-lap at 1km — alerts you when each run km is done
 Battery life — minimum 3 hours to cover the warmup and race
 Durability — it’ll go through sled pushes , carries , and rope pulls
 A Note on Indoor GPS
 HYROX races take place indoors, which reduces GPS accuracy. Some watches handle this better than others by using accelerometer data to supplement GPS. For indoor accuracy, Garmin and Polar generally outperform Apple Watch and cheaper options.
 Best GPS Watches for HYROX
 Best Overall: Garmin Forerunner 265
 The best balance of features, accuracy, and price for most HYROX athletes. AMOLED display, excellent GPS, optical heart rate, training load monitoring, and a battery life of 13 hours in GPS mode — more than enough for any HYROX race.

 Multi-band GPS — best indoor accuracy available

 Best Mid-Range: Garmin Forerunner 165

 Can I wear my watch during the sled push and carries?

 If you want a running watch without spending a fortune, you don't necessarily have to compromise on the things that matter. Today's cheaper running watches can track your pace, distance and heart rate, follow structured workouts, map your routes and give you enough training data to help you get fitter and faster. The trick is knowing which features are actually useful and which aren't worth paying extra for.
 That's where this guide comes in. We've tested and reviewed a wide range of running watches from Garmin , Coros, Amazfit, Apple and Fitbit , putting them through their paces to see how they perform when you're actually out running, rather than judging them on specifications alone. We've considered GPS accuracy, heart-rate tracking, battery life, training tools, comfort and ease of use, as well as how much watch you're getting for your money.
 And "cheap" doesn't necessarily mean bargain-basement here. We've included everything from genuinely affordable options to more advanced running watches that still offer brilliant value compared with the premium models. So whether you're looking for your first running watch, upgrading from a basic fitness tracker or want a capable training companion without spending hundreds, we've picked out the watches that are worth your money and explained who each one is best suited to.
 Read on for our top cheap running watches, plus our advice on what to look for before you buy.

 The Coros Pace 4 is a lightweight running watch that uses dual-band GPS for more accurate tracking and delivers excellent battery life in a simple, performance-focused package. It’s aimed at runners who care more about accurate tracking and long battery life than smartwatch extras, and it does that job very well for the price.
 In testing, it connected with GPS very quickly, even in tricky environments like around lots of tall buildings, and delivered consistent distance and pace data during runs. At just 32g, it’s genuinely easy to forget you’re wearing it, and that small weight makes it especially comfortable for long sessions and 24/7 use.
 Compared with cheaper Amazfit models (like the Amazfit Active 2 below), the Pace 4 is the more serious training tool, particularly when it comes to GPS reliability and longer battery life. Against Garmin’s mid-range watches, it holds its own on core running features, but Garmin still has the advantage when it comes to smartwatch-style extras like music, payments, and offline maps.
 The Pace 4 now takes the top spot as our best overall pick, replacing the older Coros Pace 3 . The Pace 3 is still a really great value buy and is now often discounted since the newer model launched, but the Pace 4 is the more refined, all-round option and the better fit for most runners.

How Amazfit has done this is a mystery, but it certainly helps with navigation during complex routes.
